The light on our home page copies something Peter made for Marta: a hexagon of 294 small triangular mirrors, each about an inch on a side, set in a 3D-printed frame. Held in the sun at the right height above the ground, it throws 294 patches of light, and the patches spell out a message.

This post explains how that works, and how the copy on the home page works.

## One mirror

A flat mirror sends light away at the same angle it arrives. To send sunlight to a chosen spot, tilt the mirror so that its normal points halfway between the sun and the spot:

$$
\hat{\mathbf n} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf s} + \hat{\mathbf t}}{\lVert \hat{\mathbf s} + \hat{\mathbf t} \rVert},
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf s}$ points from the mirror toward the sun and $\hat{\mathbf t}$ points from the mirror toward the spot. Work that out for each of the 294 mirrors and every patch of light lands where it should.

## Which mirror lights which spot

The hard part is choosing which mirror lights which spot. Any mirror can be tilted to reach any spot, so there are $294! \approx 10^{600}$ ways to pair them up. At exactly the design height, all of them make the same picture.

Most of them fall apart if the ground is a little nearer or farther. Each patch then lands short of its spot or past it, by an amount that depends on where its mirror sits in the hexagon. If the spots next to each other in a letter get their light from mirrors next to each other, those misses are alike, and the letters stay readable.

Peter looked for a good pairing with simulated annealing, run in parallel on MIT's SuperCloud cluster. It went through about 50 billion pairings before the frame was printed.

## The copy on the home page

The home page does the same thing in two dimensions. A reflected ray travels in a straight line, so a patch that is a fraction $s$ of the way from its mirror $\mathbf m_i$ to its spot $\mathbf t_i$ is at

$$
\mathbf p_i(s) = (1 - s)\,\mathbf m_i + s\,\mathbf t_i .
$$

At $s = 0$ the patches still make the hexagon, at $s = 1$ they spell the word, and past $1$ the word grows and loosens. The slider under the picture sets $s$.

The 294 spots are spread evenly along "hello" in a single-stroke script, one of the line fonts Allen Hershey designed in the 1960s for early computer displays. The pairing does not come from annealing. SciPy's `linear_sum_assignment` solves the assignment problem exactly, finding the pairing with the least total squared distance between mirrors and spots, in well under a second:

```python
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment

gap = mirror[:, None, :] - target[None, :, :]  # every mirror to every spot
cost = (gap**2).sum(-1)
rows, cols = linear_sum_assignment(cost)
target = target[cols[np.argsort(rows)]]
```

That is not the goal Peter optimized for, but it has a similar effect: nearby spots tend to get their light from nearby mirrors, so the word stays readable for a while on either side of $s = 1$.

Each patch is drawn as a soft triangle, and it gets softer the farther it travels, because sunlight comes from the whole disc of the sun. Where patches overlap, their light adds up, which is why the crossings in the letters glow.

The script that makes the data is [`_tools/mirror_points.py`](https://github.com/peterdsharpe/family-website/blob/main/_tools/mirror_points.py), and the drawing is [`assets/mirror.js`](https://github.com/peterdsharpe/family-website/blob/main/assets/mirror.js). The real mirror's design code is in [peterdsharpe/mirror-array](https://github.com/peterdsharpe/mirror-array).
